archetype.name: Playoff Team (ball-control, third-down defense)
archetype.definition: A legitimately good, not great, team that wins by holding the ball and getting off the field on third down, with a record running a little ahead of its margin and a turnover problem it has so far survived.

report.headline: Built more soundly than last year's 11-win team, despite the turnovers
report.take:
Year two under Ben Johnson looks like the opposite of year one. The 2025 Bears won 11 games on borrowed time: the best turnover differential in the league, wins well beyond their point margin, and a defense 21st in EPA allowed. This team gives the ball away constantly, with a turnover margin 29th in the league, yet sits 9th in net EPA with a top-10 defense. Last year's record leaned on luck. This one has real efficiency under it.

The engine is a defense that ends drives. Opponents convert 22.8% of third downs, the best rate in the league. The Bears have the second-best sack rate and allow the second-lowest EPA on short throws, so quick, patient offenses get nowhere. On offense they rank 3rd in yards per game and 1st in time of possession. Caleb Williams holds the ball longer than any passer in the league, and the line still allows the 6th-lowest pressure rate, which says a lot about the protection. Special teams, 4th in EPA, add hidden yardage. The quarterback carousel explains the early wobble. Case Keenum won both of his starts. Tyson Bagent's lone start was the 7-31 collapse in Green Bay with five giveaways. Williams' only loss was the 3-9 grinder against Minnesota's top-ranked defense.

What the record hides is the gap between yards and efficiency, and between wins and margin. The offense is only 14th in pass EPA and 15th in rush EPA, so the yardage comes as much from volume and possession as from explosive play. The point differential implies 6 wins, not 8, and a 75% one-score win rate has smoothed that over. The last two weeks were warnings. Five turnovers against Tampa Bay and a punchless offense against New Orleans produced two wins that failed to cover as big favorites. The 19 giveaways are the ugliest number on the sheet. Turnover rates swing hard year to year, though, so that is the stat most likely to improve.

The schedule turns brutal from here. The Bears play Detroit twice, Buffalo, Jacksonville, Green Bay, and a Minnesota defense that already held them to 3 points. They are tied with Detroit atop the NFC North. A clean-ball version of this team is a division winner. One that keeps giving the ball away five times a game will drop some of the coin-flips it has been winning.

strengths.title: Third downs end drives
strengths.body: No defense gets off the field better on third down, and the pass rush finishes drives with the second-best sack rate. Short throws are dead on arrival. The defense keeps everything underneath and wins on the late downs. A sack-driven, third-down-driven profile is fairly sticky, more so than one built on takeaways.

strengths.title: Possession offense with clean pockets
strengths.body: The Bears are 3rd in yards per game and 1st in time of possession, which shortens games for opposing offenses. Williams holds the ball longer than any QB in the league, yet the line allows the 6th-lowest pressure rate. That protection makes the patient, downfield-looking approach workable. As long as the line holds, this travels.

strengths.title: Special teams as hidden yardage
strengths.body: Special teams rank 4th in EPA per game, a steady source of field position for an offense that grinds rather than strikes. It matters most in the close games this team keeps playing.

concerns.title: Giveaways in bunches
concerns.body: The Bears have 19 turnovers in 10 games and a turnover margin 29th in the league. They come in clusters: five at Green Bay and five more against Tampa Bay. Some of it was the Bagent start, but the Tampa game was a Williams game. Turnover rates tend to regress toward average, so this should ease. Until it does, it is the fastest way for a good team to lose to anyone.

concerns.title: The deep ball gets through
concerns.body: The coverage that smothers short throws leaks badly vertically: 31st in EPA allowed on deep passes. That is the cost of a defense built to rally and tackle underneath. Against a quarterback who can push the ball, especially with Kyler Gordon out at corner, it is the obvious pressure point.

concerns.title: Record ahead of the margin
concerns.body: The point differential implies 6 wins, and the team has 2 wins over expected, 4th-most in the league. Winning three of every four one-score games is partly execution and partly fortune. Some of those close games will flip, especially against the coming schedule.

trend.note: The early weeks swung with the quarterback carousel, from 59 points in Carolina to 3 against Minnesota and a 31-7 loss in Green Bay. Williams' return brought a run of covers, but the offense has gone flat the last two weeks, with negative passing EPA in both games despite wins.

nextGame.headline: Thanksgiving in Detroit: Goff's arm against Chicago's soft deep coverage
nextGame.body:
Two 8-2 teams meet indoors on a short week with the division lead at stake, and the Book makes the Bears 2.5-point road favorites with a 55.5 total. Detroit is a mirror image of Chicago. The Lions have a top-5 offense by play-by-play EPA, 3rd in passing EPA, and a defense 30th in EPA allowed. Offenses throw on Detroit more than almost anyone, the 2nd-strongest pass funnel, and tight ends have feasted, with the TE1 role 31st in EPA allowed. That points straight at Colston Loveland, second on the team in targets. Detroit's real defensive strength is the rush, 2nd in sacks, and its run defense is respectable. Chicago's path is through the air, not on the ground.

Availability tilts slightly toward Chicago. Detroit lost center Cade Mays to injured reserve. Safety Chuck Clark, a 91%-snap starter, missed Monday's walkthrough with a hamstring, which matters against a tight-end-heavy passing attack. Sam LaPorta was limited with an ankle, DJ Wonnum sat out, and corner Ennis Rakestraw is out. On the Bears' side, Kyler Gordon is out, which thins the coverage against Detroit's deep passing. Starting tackle Theo Benedet is questionable with a quad, and his status matters against a top-2 sack defense.

waysToWin.title: Loveland and the seams
waysToWin.body: Detroit is among the worst in the league against tight ends and gets thrown on heavily, and Clark's hamstring could leave a hole at safety. A steady diet of Loveland and the middle of the field lets Williams avoid the edge rushers while moving the chains.

waysToWin.title: Win third down on both sides
waysToWin.body: Detroit allows the 6th-worst third-down conversion rate, while the Bears allow the league's lowest. If Chicago sustains drives and wins the possession game as usual, Goff's offense gets fewer chances to turn this into the shootout the total implies.

waysToWin.title: Rush Goff with Mays out
waysToWin.body: Detroit's protection rates well on pressure but sits only 19th in sack rate, and it is missing its center. The Bears' 2nd-ranked sack rate can end drives before the deep shots develop.

waysToLose.title: Goff beats them over the top
waysToLose.body: Detroit's passing attack is 3rd in EPA, and the Bears' deep coverage is 31st, now without Gordon. A couple of explosive completions erase the clock advantage Chicago works so hard to build.

waysToLose.title: Another turnover cluster
waysToLose.body: Detroit doesn't take the ball away much, 25th in takeaways, so any giveaways here would be self-inflicted. The Bears have already had two five-turnover games, and against an offense this good, short fields are fatal.

waysToLose.title: The pass rush wins the edges
waysToLose.body: Detroit is 2nd in sacks, and Benedet is questionable on a short week. Williams' long time to throw is an asset behind a healthy line but a liability if a tackle is missing.

nextGame.watch: How often Williams finds Loveland over the middle, and whether Detroit's safety group, possibly without Clark, can stop it.

restOfSeason.body:
The defensive structure should hold: elite third-down defense and a top-3 sack rate are skills, not bounces. The turnover margin is the likeliest number to improve, because few teams stay this careless. Expect the giveaways to ease, which would make the offense's yardage turn into points more reliably. The pull the other way is the close-game record. The margin says 6 wins, and the one-score games won't all keep breaking Chicago's way.

The schedule is the real story. Of the six games after Thanksgiving, only Miami is soft, and the Bears face two top-2 defenses (Jacksonville and Minnesota) plus Buffalo on the road. With Detroit tied atop the division, the two Lions games likely decide the NFC North. The likeliest finish is double-digit wins and a playoff berth, with the division a coin flip.
swingFactors: Results in the two Detroit games

confidence.note: Ten games split across three QBs; efficiency is solid but the record leans on close wins.
